id: Memory of the Murdered Professors at the Jagiellonian

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

After Hasior They fired a bullet into the head of each question, trying to kill Kant’s unending argument with Hegel. They burned laws, moral codes, & the Golden Means. Anyone serving tea & cookies to Death, looking or acting as if he knew love, stood before the firing squad. All questions had to go. Pronoun or noun. If it crawled on busted kneecaps, whimpering & begging for mercy, it was still half of a question. * * *The little skyscraper of glass boxes sunlight strikes the same time of day at a certain angle outside Zakopane looks like condos where nimble ghosts still stand up to the darkest answers. No, I can’t hear one voice pleading. But I do hear gusts coming down from the hills. No, you’re wrong again. The crow perched on the totem is real. Look at how the light lifts off its wings, but I wish I could understand what it is he’s trying to say. I think I heard a name.

Addressing the systematic and violent eradication of philosophical inquiry, ethics, and fundamental human questions, the text explores this trauma through poetic observations of artist Władysław Hasior's glass-box structures in the landscape of Zakopane. It reveals that despite brutal attempts to enforce absolute answers and eliminate doubt, resilient ghostly presences and symbolic natural forms endure, signifying that human memory and the search for meaning cannot be entirely destroyed.

outputs.L1:
Here are two polished options. Because the original text is deeply poetic, surreal, and philosophical (referencing the Polish artist Władysław Hasior, Kant, Hegel, and Zakopane), these revisions enhance the literary cadence, grammar, and flow while keeping every image and thought intact.

### Option 1: Literary & Evocative (Recommended)
> After Hasior, they put a bullet through the head of every question, attempting to extinguish the endless debate between Kant and Hegel. They burned laws, moral codes, and the Golden Mean. Anyone who served tea and cookies to Death, or who looked and acted as though he knew love, was placed before the firing squad. Every question had to be eliminated—pronoun or noun alike. Even if it crawled on shattered knees, whimpering and begging for mercy, it remained half a question.
> 
> \* \* \*
> 
> Outside Zakopane, a small skyscraper of glass boxes catches the sunlight at the exact same angle and hour each day. It resembles condominiums where nimble ghosts still stand against the darkest answers. No, I cannot hear a single voice pleading, though I do hear the gusts rushing down from the hills. No, you are wrong again: the crow perched atop the totem is real. Look at how the light lifts off its wings. I only wish I could comprehend what he is trying to say. I think I heard a name.

---

### Option 2: Refined & Dramatic
> In the wake of Hasior, they executed every question, seeking to silence Kant’s eternal argument with Hegel. They consigned laws, moral codes, and the Golden Mean to the flames. Anyone serving tea and cookies to Death, or bearing the countenance of one who knew love, stood before the firing squad. All questions were marked for destruction, whether pronoun or noun. Even if it crawled on broken knees, whimpering and pleading for mercy, it was still half a question.
> 
> \* \* \*
> 
> Outside Zakopane, a modest glass tower catches the sunlight at a precise angle every afternoon, looking like modern condos where agile ghosts still rise against the darkest answers. No, I cannot hear a voice pleading; I hear only the wind coming down from the hills. No, you are mistaken once more. The crow perched on the totem is real—observe the light reflecting off its wings. Yet, I wish I could decipher what he seeks to convey. I believe I heard a name.

### Key Improvements Made:
* **Punctuation & Flow:** Fixed run-on sentences, awkward capitalizations (e.g., *"After Hasior They"*), and ambiguous phrasing (e.g., *"glass boxes sunlight strikes"*).
* **Elevated Vocabulary:** Refined informal phrases like *"busted kneecaps"* to *"shattered knees"* or *"broken knees"* to match the heavy, philosophical tone of the piece.
* **Preserved Context:** Kept all original surreal imagery, philosophical references (Kant, Hegel, Golden Mean), and specific details (tea and cookies, Zakopane, the crow on the totem).
outputs.L2:
In the period following Hasior, executioners shot every single inquiry directly in the head to permanently extinguish the ongoing philosophical debate between Kant and Hegel. Flames consumed all legal statutes, ethical frameworks, and principles of moderation. A firing squad was mobilized for anyone caught offering tea and baked goods to the Grim Reaper, as well as those whose demeanor suggested familiarity with affection. Total destruction was mandated for every query, whether phrased as a noun or a pronoun. Even if an entity dragged itself along on shattered knees while weeping and begging for clemency, it still constituted half an inquiry.

* * *

Beyond Zakopane, solar beams hit a compact tower constructed from glass cubes at a precise tilt during the exact same hour daily. It resembles modern residential units where agile spirits continue to defy the most dismal conclusions. Contrary to your assumption, I do not register any individual voice begging for help, though I do hear wind sweeping down from the surrounding heights. You are mistaken once more: the crow seated atop the totem pole is tangible. Observe the way illumination glances off its plumage; I only wish I possessed the ability to decipher its intended message. It seemed as though a person's name was spoken.
outputs.L3:
It began with an unsparing cataclysm of the mind. A violent purge swept across the land, systematically dismantling every framework humanity had built to understand itself. Philosophical inquiry was dragged into the light and shattered; ancient moral codes were unspooled; laws were dissolved into anarchy; and the gentlest expressions of love and mercy were branded as weaknesses and thoroughly erased. This was not merely an attack on institutions, but an war on curiosity itself. Every form of question—every *why*, *how*, and *what if*—was hunted down like a fugitive. The enforcers of this new order operated without pity or exception, ruthlessly exterminating doubt until only a bleak, unquestioned silence remained.

Yet, complete annihilation proved impossible. High in the cold air near Zakopane, nestled against the loom of the mountains, stands a solitary glass structure. It is a striking, fragile monument amidst the ruin. Within its translucent walls, ghostly forms flicker and gather—the spectral echoes of those who dared to wonder. In this sanctuary of light and reflection, these pale phantoms continue a quiet, stubborn resistance. They gather not to offer new dogmas, but to defy the dark, absolute answers that now rule the world, holding open the space for mystery and doubt.

Below this mountain haven, the voices of the living have gone silent. Human pleas, once carried on prayers and tears, can no longer be heard across the barren plains. But the earth itself has stepped into the void. Where human speech was stolen, the natural landscape has found a voice. A constant, mournful wind blows down from the high hills, rushing through the pines and canyons, acting as a surrogate tongue for a silenced species. The land speaks what people no longer can.

Standing in the shadow of this transformed world, I watch and listen. My eyes fix upon a real crow, perched motionless atop a rough-hewn totem. It is a creature of flesh and blood, a stark black smudge against the gray sky. As it caws into the rushing wind, I lean in close, striving with all my remaining spirit to decipher the mysterious message it conveys—searching the bird's ancient, dark gaze for the lost name of a world that once dared to ask why.
outputs.L4:
**Vitrines of the Unanswered: Memory and Eradication in Zakopane**

There is a subtle, terrible violence in the murder of the question mark. Throughout history, regimes of absolute certainty have sought to level the delicate architecture of human thought, systematically razing the spaces where ethics, doubt, and philosophical inquiry reside. This violence does not merely aim to conquer territory or subjugate bodies; it attempts a far more total annihilation—the eradication of the human capacity to ask *why*. In place of open-minded reflection, brutal dogmas enforce mandatory answers, seeking to flatten the landscape of human consciousness into a desert of forced obedience.

Yet, trauma leaves a geography behind, and the suppressed spirit has a way of haunting the edges of its forced silence. High in the cold, misty expanse of Zakopane, where the rugged Tatra Mountains rise like ancient sentinels, this wound finds a profoundly poetic voice in the work of artist Władysław Hasior. 

Hasior’s glass-box structures, scattered throughout this dramatic landscape, act as transparent reliquaries for a damaged collective soul. Encased within their fragile walls are assemblages of the broken and the discarded: melted wax, scorched wood, rusted iron, scraps of fabric, bone, and fractured mirrors. These glass vitrines stand as silent witnesses in the open air, positioned precisely where human trauma confronts the indifferent, elemental majesty of nature. 

To observe these structures in the wild, shifting weather of Zakopane is to witness a quiet rebellion against total erasure. The glass creates a paradoxical barrier: it isolates the tragic relics of human violence, yet leaves them completely exposed to the light, snow, and mountain mist. The attempt by authoritarian ideologies to enforce absolute answers is rendered absurd beside these fragile boxes. Try as the purges might to eliminate uncertainty, Hasior’s glass captures shadow and fog, transforming condensation into weeping walls and reflections into ghostly presences that hover between the interior art and the exterior wilderness.

Nature itself becomes a co-conspirator in this act of memory. As moss edges around the iron borders of the glass and the mountain wind whistles through the surrounding pines, the environment adopts the unmoored questions that humans were forbidden to speak. The violent suppression of philosophy fails because the urge to seek meaning is not merely an intellectual exercise; it is an elemental force, as persistent as the mountain water cutting through granite.

Ultimately, Hasior’s glass boxes reveal that absolute power suffers from a fatal blindness. It assumes that by destroying the thinker, it destroys the thought; that by outlawing ethics, it erases the human instinct for justice. But in the quiet, atmospheric heights of Zakopane, the ghostly forms trapped in glass endure. They remind us that memory cannot be buried deep enough, nor can doubt be burned away entirely. Even in the wake of the most violent silences, the sanctuary of human inquiry remains unbroken, holding its fragile, persistent light against the dark.
outputs.L5:
Long **after** the flames of his iconic outdoor installations had faded into ash, the visionary realm of Władysław **Hasior** remained indelible in the minds of those who witnessed it. 

Standing before his surreal assemblages—striking constructs forged from discarded metal, broken glass, worn textiles, and forgotten relics—viewers were forced to confront a raw, poetic history. **They** watched as everyday objects, stripped of their original utility, were resurrected into tragic, mythological figures that seemed to whisper secrets of memory and human suffering. 

**After** spending time in the presence of his art, visitors rarely looked at the world the same way again. In the quiet stillness of the gallery, **they** realized that even in the debris of human existence, sacred stories were waiting to be told.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem inspired by Polish artist Władysław Hasior, combining themes of totalitarian suppression of philosophy (Kant vs. Hegel) with vivid imagery of Zakopane, glass structures, and a crow on a totem.
counterfactuals.output:
In the shadow of the Sleeping Knight, where the Tatra granite bleeds turpentine into the snow, they erected the cathedral of crushed syllogisms. It is an assemblage of mountain dirt and state terror, stitched together with Władysław Hasior’s rusted wire and wet red felt. Here, in the freeze of Zakopane, where the *halny* wind screams through the hollow trunks of Podhale pines, the Ministry of Truth has brought philosophy to be executed.

A sequence of glass structures rises from the frost like jagged, transparent lungs. Within the largest glass cube, Immanuel Kant’s moral sky is trapped inside a cracked mason jar—his starry heavens suffocated under a moldy layer of raw sheepskin. The Commissars have outlawed the *Critique of Pure Reason*; they have dragged the Categorical Imperative into the cold and impaled it upon a spit of pig iron. For them, the individual mind is a dangerous void, a glass coffin that must be filled with heavy, uniform concrete. 

They prefer Hegel, but only after butchering him. High on the mountain slope, they have forged his Absolute Spirit into a steam-driven dialectic made of bent iron and bicycle chains. *Thesis* is an iron boot striking the floorboards; *Antithesis* is a frozen tongue pressed against a lead pipe. There is no triumph in their *Synthesis*—only a banner of charred canvas dripping axle grease onto the pristine drifts. History does not march toward freedom here; it turns a massive, squealing gear that grinds human thought into grey enamel.

At the edge of the glass compound stands the totem: a towering, blackened beam of carved larch wood, studded with silver spoons, crushed pocket watches, and small, weeping mirrors. At its apex sits a crow with eyes made of brass boot-grommets. Its feathers are stiff with ice and old soot. In its beak, it holds a torn leaf from the *Phenomenology of Spirit*, stripping the dialectic into long, black ribbons that scatter across the timberline.

The crow does not caw; it vibrates with the sound of a muted organ. When the glass walls shudder under the pressure of the falling sky, Kant’s noumenal world shatters into thousands of blinding, crystalline needles, sticking into the mountain mud. Hegel’s iron spirit walks past on stilts of melted glass, herding the silent, wooden figures of the mountain folk toward the horizon—where reason is forbidden to burn, and only the fire of the artifice remains awake.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short piece of flash fiction about a world where an oppressive regime decides to literally execute abstract concepts like questions, laws, and love.
counterfactuals.output:
The blade of the Great Scaffold was forged from absolute silence.

First, they executed *The Question*.

They dragged it to the platform in a cage of lead—a shimmering, silver syntax that vibrated with the persistent frequencies of *Why?* and *How?* 

The Supreme Leader read the sentence from his balcony: "For the crime of destabilizing certainty."

The blade fell. The silver hook severed. 

Instantly, the faces of the assembled thousands went smooth as river stones. I looked at the woman beside me. I wanted to ask her what she thought, but the grammar had vanished from my throat. I could only state facts. *The sky is gray. The crowd is large.* The urge to know anything beyond what was presented simply evaporated, leaving our minds as flat and featureless as frozen ponds.

A month later, they executed *Law*.

They did not burn books; they brought forth the abstract lattice of order itself, a glowing, geometric web that held the boundaries between right, wrong, mine, and yours. The Executioner shattered it with an iron mallet.

When the lattice splintered into dust, my neighbor reached over and took my coat. I felt no indignation. Theft was no longer a concept; there was no law to break, no right to assert. There was only the physical reality of his cold hands and my bare shoulders. Power became the only gravity left in the world.

Finally, on a freezing Tuesday, they brought out *Love*.

It did not look like a heart. It looked like a tangled thread of spun warmth, smelling of rain and old paper, pulsing with a deep, rhythmic violet light. It fought the chains, humming a frequency that made the spectators’ chests ache with a sudden, agonizing memory of light.

"Love makes men weak," the Supreme Leader announced through the loudspeakers. "Love makes a man prefer a person over the State."

I stood in the square, my hand clasped in Elena’s. Our fingers were intertwined by muscle memory, though we no longer had the words to ask why we stood together. 

The Executioner raised his axe.

A sudden wind swept the square. The axe descended.

The thread snapped. A sharp, violent suction filled the air, as if a vital element had been ripped from the atmosphere. The violet light flared once, turned to gray ash, and scattered into the mud.

I turned to look at Elena.

Her hand was still in mine. It was flesh. Five digits. A skin temperature of roughly ninety-eight degrees. 

I looked into her eyes. They were brown optics catching the overcast light. That was all. There was no pull, no ache, no phantom impulse to shield her from a falling stone. She was merely a mass of cell tissue occupying a coordinate adjacent to mine. 

High above us, the Supreme Leader leaned over the velvet railing of his balcony. He raised his arms, waiting for the crowd to shift its boundless, redirected devotion toward him. He waited for the deafening cheers of a people who now belonged entirely to the State.

But he had miscalculated the math of the block.

Ten thousand people stood in the square, staring up at him with blank, unblinking eyes. 

We did not hate him. We did not love him. We had no laws to compel our obedience, no questions to prompt our action, and no love to offer an idol.

The Supreme Leader opened his mouth to give a command, but in a world without questions, no one listened; in a world without law, no one obeyed; and in a world without love, no one cared.

We simply stood there, motionless, as the snow began to fall.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: You are a contemporary avant-garde poet. Channel a bleak, Eastern European surrealist style in a prose poem about the murder of dialectics, modern architecture in the Tatra mountains, and wind coming off the hills.
counterfactuals.output:
The wind coming off the granite ridges does not carry news; it carries teeth. It smells of wet sheepskin, ozone, and iron rust, whistling through the empty concrete honeycombs of the new sanatorium. High above the timberline, where the dwarf pines grow crooked out of spite, a brutalist wedge of grey cement has been driven into the mountain’s flank—an angular, six-story tooth thrusting toward a sky the color of a wet zinc bucket. 

Behind the boiler room, where the iron pipes sweat grease into the mud, they killed Dialectics. It was not a grand historical execution. There were no brass bands, no fiery manifestos, no third term rising like a red bird from the rubble. Thesis sat on a turned-over bucket, gnawing on a turnip; Antithesis lay in the drainage ditch with its throat cut by a broken vodka bottle. When the two finally collided, they did not ignite the future—they merely formed a dark, jelly-like clot. Synthesis was strangled at birth by an official in a stained trench coat who promptly filed a three-part form requesting more gravel for the road. 

Now the wind—the violent, suffocating *halny*—roars down the gulley, bending the television antennas until they snap like dried coriander. It drives snow into the smoked-glass balconies, sweeping away the last fragments of cause and effect. Inside the dining hall, tourists silently chew their lard-bread beneath neon tubes that hum in a minor key. They watch the fog erase the sharp, modern edges of the hotel, one balcony at a time. The mountain does not care that the contradiction was left unhandled; it simply opens its grey mouth and breathes another gale down the pass, filling the empty culverts with cold, unreasoning foam.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem containing these elements: Kant and Hegel's unending argument, firing squads shooting at questions, glass boxes outside Zakopane, and a crow perched on a totem that seems to be trying to speak.
counterfactuals.output: Outside Zakopane, where the black spruces scrape against a low sky the color of zinc, a row of empty glass boxes sits in the frost, holding nothing but the cold architecture of their own transparency. It is here that Kant and Hegel maintain their unending argument, pacing the perimeter of the enclosures. Kant traces the glass with a gloved finger, insisting on the absolute gulf between the sight of the mountain and the mountain itself, while Hegel sweeps past in a heavy, snow-laden coat, shouting that the barrier is merely a moment of spirit waiting to digest its own negation. They pay no mind to the dawn, when masked firing squads march into the glade to line up before the air itself, raising their rifles to shoot at questions drifting like suspended breath. *Why?* *For whom?* *To what end?* The volleys shatter the silence, lead tearing through the syntax of curiosity, but the interrogation marks simply reassemble behind the drifting cordite smoke, unhurt, bleeding only ink onto the frozen ground. High above the gunfire and the endless loop of the philosophers' debate, a crow sits anchored to the head of a rotting cedar totem. Its obsidian feathers are stiff with ice, its throat working in frantic, muscular ripples as its beak opens and closes, clicking against the stillness, straining with a human and desperate agony to finally utter the single word that will end the world.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a dark, surrealist paragraph about the end of thought and morality.
counterfactuals.output: In the quiet belly of the cosmic abattoir, the last human idea curled like a scorched worm and dissolved into a pool of warm, grey oil. Morality—that ancient, gilded skeleton—crumbled into a fine dust, its rusted scales of judgment swallowed by a sky that wept blind, toothless mouths. Right and Wrong, once warring stars, bled into one another until they formed a sickening, indifferent violet, rendering the saint and the butcher indistinguishable beneath the glare of an unblinking moon. Logic unraveled into threads of black bile, spilling from the ears of stone statues that had forgotten how to cast a shadow. Here, in the soft, rotting marrow of absolute silence, the sin was identical to the prayer, and the mind was merely a hollow bell submerged in tar, echoing nothing, wanting nothing, forever un-thinking itself into the neutral void.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
